name: Caffeine
summary: The most used psychoactive substance on earth, and the one with the tidiest pharmacokinetics: it is absorbed almost completely, spreads through total body water, and is cleared by a single enzyme at a steady proportional rate.
mechanism: Blocks adenosine A1 and A2A receptors. Adenosine builds up through the day and signals sleep pressure; caffeine occupies the receptors without activating them, so the signal goes unheard. The adenosine itself keeps accumulating, which is why the tiredness arrives all at once when the caffeine clears.

oral.note: Essentially complete absorption with no measurable first-pass loss; the liver clears it slowly enough that nearly all of it survives the first trip through.

pathways.name: Paraxanthine
pathways.note: The main metabolite, and itself a stimulant and adenosine blocker. A good share of what you feel in the later hours is paraxanthine, not caffeine.

pathways.name: Theobromine
pathways.note: The compound that makes up most of chocolate's mild lift. Weak stimulant, a vasodilator, half-life around 7 hours.

pathways.name: Theophylline
pathways.note: A bronchodilator still used as an asthma drug. The same molecule, just a different methyl group missing.

effect_levels.label: Toxic range reported in the literature

smoker.note: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke induce CYP1A2, roughly doubling caffeine clearance. This is why heavy smokers drink more coffee, and why quitting raises caffeine levels sharply on the same intake — a known cause of the jitters in the first week off cigarettes.

oral_contraceptives.note: Ethinylestradiol inhibits CYP1A2; the half-life roughly doubles.

pregnancy_third_trimester.note: CYP1A2 activity falls steeply; the half-life can reach 15 hours or more.

liver_cirrhosis.note: Clearance depends almost entirely on hepatic enzyme capacity, so it falls with it.
